Read About Havana

A city that was the richest port in the Spanish empire, then the most glamorous gambling resort in the hemisphere, then the world's most improbable communist experiment — and remains, against all of it, genuinely beautiful.

The city Spain couldn't afford to lose

Havana was founded in 1519 by a conquistador named Pánfilo de Narváez, moved twice before settling on the natural harbor that everyone who arrived could see was the best anchorage in the Caribbean, and within a generation had become the most strategically important city in the Spanish empire. Every year, the combined fleets of New Spain and Peru — the treasure fleets carrying silver from Potosí and gold from Mexico — stopped in Havana before making the crossing to Seville. The city was not the origin of the wealth; it was the valve that controlled it.

This position made Havana worth attacking and worth defending, repeatedly. The Spanish built El Morro, the fortress guarding the harbor entrance, in 1589. They spent the next two centuries adding Fortaleza de la Cabaña on the ridge behind it and a chain of smaller fortifications around the bay. Then the British captured the whole thing in 1762, held it for eleven months, and gave it back to Spain in exchange for Florida. The eleven months mattered. The British opened Havana's port to free trade — forbidden under Spanish mercantilist restrictions — and 700 ships arrived in the time Spain had spent debating their next move. Havana learned something in that year that Spain never wanted it to learn.

What grew in the centuries after was a city of enormous civic ambition. The Plaza de la Catedral — the baroque square you'll walk on Day 2 — was built in the 18th century and has not fundamentally changed since. The neoclassical domes and arcaded boulevards of the old city, the marble floors of the colonial palaces, the Paseo del Prado modeled on Las Ramblas — this was a colonial capital at the height of its confidence, and the confidence is still legible in every façade.

The long fall and the moment it crystallized

Spain held Cuba until 1898, longer than any other American colony, largely because the sugar economy that replaced the treasure fleets was too valuable to relinquish and too entangled with the slave trade to release easily. The Ten Years' War (1868–78) and the Final War of Independence (1895–98) destroyed huge parts of the island. The United States intervened at the end, took the credit for the victory, and administered Cuba as a protectorate under the Platt Amendment — which gave Washington the right to intervene in Cuban affairs whenever it judged it necessary — until 1934.

The republic that followed was unstable, lurching between reformist governments and coups. Fulgencio Batista staged his first coup in 1933, led a relatively reformist period through 1944, watched the constitutional governments of Grau San Martín and Prío Socarrás struggle with corruption, and in 1952 staged his second coup — canceling the elections in which Fidel Castro, then a young Havana lawyer, was a congressional candidate.

Batista's second rule made Havana the entertainment capital of the American mafia. Meyer Lansky ran the Riviera. The Nacional attracted Frank Sinatra and Marlene Dietrich. The casinos were everywhere, the corruption absolute, and the countryside — growing sugar cane for American companies at starvation wages — was an entirely different country. In December 1956, Castro and eighty-one others landed on the south coast from a leaking yacht called Granma. Eighty of them were killed or captured within days. The twelve survivors walked into the Sierra Maestra mountains and started a guerrilla campaign that took the capital on January 1, 1959.

The city the Revolution preserved by accident

What happened to Havana after 1959 is, architecturally, one of the stranger stories in urban history. The revolutionary government nationalised property, redirected resources to the countryside, ended the casino economy, and stopped the flow of American capital and tourism that had been driving Havana's development. The city froze. The grand hotels didn't get new lobbies. The colonial mansions didn't get demolished for office towers. The Art Deco apartment buildings on the Malecón didn't get replaced by glass curtain walls. The money ran out, and then the US embargo locked the money out.

The result — unintended, lamented by the Cubans who watch the buildings decay, celebrated by the architectural historians who watch the same buildings survive — is a city with the highest concentration of pre-1960 architecture in the western hemisphere. Old Havana was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982. The Cuban Heritage Office (OHCH), funded partly by tourism revenue, has been restoring the colonial core since the early 1980s with serious scholarship and visible results. The restoration is ongoing, uneven, and sometimes makes things worse, as restorations do. But what it's working with is real.

Walk any block in Habana Vieja and you're passing through continuous inhabitation since the 16th century — a city where the infrastructure failed before the architecture did, which is the only reason the architecture survived.

The Malecón, and what it means to sit there

The Malecón was built between 1901 and 1952, a sea wall and broad promenade running eight kilometres from the mouth of the harbor around the north coast of the city to the Vedado district. It faces north, into the Florida Straits and the Gulf Stream, and in winter the waves crash over the wall and flood the lanes of the road beside it. In summer it bakes. At any hour, any day, any weather, there are people sitting on it — fishing, talking, watching the water, playing guitars, waiting for nothing. Habaneros call it the city's living room, which is accurate but doesn't capture the specific quality of it: the sense that the city's private life is conducted on a concrete wall exposed to the open sea.

In 1994, when the Special Period — the economic crisis that followed the Soviet collapse — was at its worst, tens of thousands of Cubans lashed together rafts from inner tubes and oil drums and launched themselves from the Malecón toward Florida, 145 kilometres across the Straits. An estimated 30,000 made the crossing that year. An unknown number didn't. The Malecón has been the departure point for every generation of Cubans who decided the gap between what Cuba was and what it might be was too wide to wait for. People still sit on it every evening, watching the same water.

Vedado, and where the city was trying to go

Vedado is where Havana planned its future and then ran out of century to build it in. Developed from the 1860s onward on what had been a forest west of Centro Habana, Vedado was laid out on a regular grid with wide, tree-lined streets and large residential lots — the Cuban upper class building a district modeled on American and European ideas of how a modern city should look. The Hotel Nacional went up in 1930 on the clifftop overlooking the sea. The Focsa building — 35 floors, completed in 1956, still one of the largest reinforced concrete structures built in the Americas at the time — dominates the skyline. The Tribunal de Cuentas, the Radiocentro, the ministry buildings: Vedado in the 1950s was building itself into a genuine mid-century metropolis.

Then it stopped. The Focsa's upper floors went dark. The grands projets of the republican era — the tunnel under the harbor, the University of Havana stadium — were finished; the next wave never started. Vedado today is a city district in arrested mid-development, which gives it a particular character: the tree-lined streets and the Art Deco mansions divided into apartments, the weight of the 1950s still everywhere, the absence of the 1970s and 1980s that a functioning economy would have layered over it.

Viñales, and what lies an hour and a half behind the city

The road west from Havana runs through the tobacco fields of Pinar del Río province and climbs into a landscape that bears no relation to the coastal city you left. The Valle de Viñales is a UNESCO World Heritage Site not for its colonial architecture or its historical significance but for what the earth itself did here: limestone formations called mogotes — steep-sided remnants of a plateau that eroded away around them over millions of years — rise from the red soil in sheer-faced humps, some reaching 300 metres, clothed in palms and tree ferns. The valley floor between them grows the tobacco that Cuba uses for its premium cigars: the Vuelta Abajo, the narrow band of soil the Habano industry maintains was never matched anywhere else in the world.

Viñales is 130 kilometres from Havana and connected by a decent two-lane road. The village at its center — colonial wooden buildings on arcaded streets, painted in the faded blues and greens of a place that was not wealthy enough to modernise — has been a tourist destination since the 1990s and remains low-key enough that the valley still feels primarily like a place people live in. The tobacco farmers are real. The horses in the fields are real. The Cueva del Indio, the cave the Taíno people used before the Spanish arrived, is a hole in the limestone you take a boat through. These things existed long before anyone built a tourist infrastructure around them and will continue to exist after it changes again.

Before you go

Three things that are more useful to know before you arrive than after. The currency situation: Cuba's dual-currency system ended in 2021, leaving the Cuban Peso (CUP) as the only legal tender. US cards and US dollars are problematic — the USD attracts a 10% surcharge when exchanged, and US-issued cards are blocked entirely. Bring EUR, Canadian dollars, or British pounds in cash and exchange at a CADECA office for the best rate. The internet situation: connectivity is state-controlled, slow, and patchy. Wi-fi exists in hotels and at Etecsa hotspots in public squares; buy a NAUTA card. Plan your day before you leave the hotel, not on the street. The transportation situation: there are no ride apps. Cubataxi metered cabs are reliable; agree the fare first, or confirm the meter is running.

The other thing — less practical, more essential — is to go without a fixed idea of what Havana should feel like. The city has been described so many times in terms of its nostalgia and its decay that it's easy to arrive looking for a ruin with good mojitos. What you'll find is a city of 2.1 million people conducting ordinary lives in extraordinary surroundings, under conditions of chronic material scarcity, with a social intelligence and a musicality that are genuinely their own and not performed for the visitor. Pay attention to that rather than the classic cars.
